t.6.41.1: Then Rāvaṇa, together with the rākṣasas, heard the most tumultuous clamor of those swift and mighty monkeys as they roared.
t.6.41.2: Having heard that loud uproar, resounding deep and rich, he then spoke these words in the midst of his ministers.
t.6.41.3: Since that exceedingly great roar has arisen from the many overjoyed monkeys, like that of thundering clouds,
t.6.41.5: Those two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, were bound by sharp arrows; and this very great roar seems to rouse a doubt in me.
t.6.41.4: Clearly there is very great joy among them; of this there is no doubt. For indeed, by their mighty roars the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, has been stirred into turmoil.
t.6.41.6: Having spoken these words to his ministers, the lord of the rākṣasas then addressed the nairṛtas who were moving about near him there.
t.6.41.7: Let it be found out quickly what cause for joy has arisen for all these forest-dwellers, at a time when grief has come upon them.
t.6.41.8: Thus addressed by him, they, agitated, climbed the rampart and saw the army protected by the great-souled Sugrīva.
t.6.41.9: Seeing the two illustrious Rāghavas risen up, freed from the most dreadful bond of arrows, the rākṣasas were dismayed.
t.6.41.11: The night-rangers, skilled in speech, their faces downcast, reported that whole unpleasant matter to Rāvaṇa exactly as it had happened.
t.6.41.10: Their hearts terrified at all this, they climbed down from the rampart, and all of them, with dejected faces, presented themselves before the lord of the Rākṣasas.
t.6.41.13: Freed from the bondage of arrows, those two, equal in valour to lordly elephants, are seen on the field of battle like two elephants that have broken their fetters.
t.6.41.12: Those two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who in battle had been bound by Indrajit with a binding of arrows, were left with arms unable to stir.
t.6.41.14: Having heard those words of theirs, the mighty lord of the rākṣasas, overcome by anxiety and grief, spoke with a dejected face.
t.6.41.15: Having crushed them in battle, Indrajit bound the two with terrible arrows granted as boons, unfailing, like venomous serpents and blazing like the sun.
t.6.41.16: If my two enemies have been freed after falling into that bond of weapons, then I see this whole army of mine placed in peril.
t.6.41.17: Fruitless indeed have become those arrows with the fiery might of Vāsuki, by which in battle the life of my enemies had been seized.
t.6.41.18: Having spoken thus, enraged and hissing like a serpent, he addressed, in the midst of the rākṣasas, a rākṣasa named Dhūmrākṣa.
t.6.41.19: Accompanied by a mighty army of rākṣasas of terrible deeds, go forth to slay Rāma together with the monkeys.
t.6.41.20: Thus addressed by the wise lord of the Rākṣasas, Dhūmrākṣa made obeisance and, greatly delighted, went forth from the royal palace.
t.6.41.22: Hearing the words of Dhūmrākṣa, the commander of the forces, attended by his troops, swiftly marshalled the army at the command of Rāvaṇa.
t.6.41.21: Having gone out through that gate, he said to the commander of the forces: “Quickly hasten the army, the warriors eager for battle. What is the use of delay?”
t.6.41.23: Those mighty night-roamers of terrible form, with bells tied on, roaring and thrilled with excitement, surrounded Dhūmrākṣa.
t.6.41.24: With various weapons in their hands, holding spears and hammers, they were armed in abundance with maces, axes, staves and iron clubs.
t.6.41.25: With iron clubs, javelins, broad-headed arrows, lances and axes, the terrible rākṣasas sallied forth, roaring like rain-clouds.
t.6.41.27: With exceedingly swift horses and with lordly elephants wild with rut, those tigers among rākṣasas sallied forth, unassailable like tigers.
t.6.41.26: Others, clad in armour, came forth with chariots richly adorned with banners and fitted with networks of gold, and with donkeys of many different faces.
t.6.41.28: Dhūmrākṣa, whose voice was harsh, mounted his divine chariot, yoked with donkeys adorned with gold and having the faces of wolves and lions.
t.6.41.29: The mighty Dhūmrākṣa, surrounded by rākṣasas, set forth laughing toward the western gate, where Hanūmān, the leader of the troops, stood.
t.6.41.30: But as the exceedingly dreadful rākṣasa of fearsome appearance set out, cruel birds moving through the sky tried to hold him back.
t.6.41.31: A huge and dreadful vulture swooped down upon the top of the chariot, and carrion-eaters, crowded together, descended upon the tip of the banner.
t.6.41.32: A huge white headless trunk, drenched with blood, fell to the ground close to Dhūmrākṣa, letting out a harsh, discordant cry.
t.6.41.33: The god of rain showered down blood and the earth trembled; the wind blew in a contrary direction with a roar like a thunderclap, and there the quarters, shrouded in masses of darkness, did not shine.
t.6.41.34: Then Dhūmrākṣa, seeing the terrible portents that had appeared, bringing fear to the Rākṣasas, became deeply disturbed.
t.6.41.35: Then the very fearsome and mighty one, eager for battle and surrounded by many night-rangers, sallied forth and beheld that army, abounding in monkeys and vast as the ocean, protected by the arms of Rāghava.
